turns.content:
11:42pm

Here's the full 8-stanza roast poem for Uncle Greg. Let me know if it hits hard in a good way or if I'm gonna get disowned tomorrow night lol

—

Greg turns sixty, that's the news
A walking AARP brochure
Your knees pop like bubble wrap
And your hair's joined the great escape

Remember when you tried to sell
Those air fryer widgets from your car
Lost your shirt, then lost your mind
Now you're grilling in the backyard

This is the man who bought a boat
Then realized water makes him float
Now it's parked and gathering moss
Like your ambition, like your sauce

You filed for Chapter 7 last spring
Foreclosure signs, that whole sad thing
But Greg just laughed and lit a stogie
Said "at least my credit's bogie"

Your doctor says drop fifty pounds
You say "pass the bacon rounds"
Your cholesterol's a crime scene
But hey, you're still here, it seems

Married four times, what a streak
Each one shorter than the last
Now you're dating someone named Peak
And you forgot your anniversary fast

Your kids won't text you back
You blame the iPhone, that's a fact
But Greg, the phone's not the issue
It's the decade you spent distant

So here's to sixty, here's to you
The human version of cheap stew
Still bubbling, still a mess
But somehow we love you best

This is a solid roast skeleton — the rhythm's loose in spots but the voice is right, and the closing stanza does the important work of landing on affection. A few stanzas will get laughs.

But honest read: a couple of these cross from "roast" into "airing real wounds in front of a crowd," and that's where disowning risk actually lives.

**Will probably land fine:**
- Age/knees/hair stanza — classic roast material, everyone's in on the joke
- The boat stanza — good punchline structure ("like your ambition, like your sauce" is the best line in the poem)
- The bacon/doctor stanza — standard and affectionate

**Genuinely risky:**
- **Chapter 7 / foreclosure stanza.** If the bankruptcy is real and recent, reading it aloud at a party — possibly with acquaintances present who didn't know — is less roast and more public humiliation. Roasts work on vanity and absurdity, not fresh financial trauma.
- **"Your kids won't text you back... the decade you spent distant."** This is the one I'd cut without hesitation. It's not a joke about Greg; it's an accusation delivered in front of the family, and it implicates his kids in the room. If there's real estrangement there, this stanza will hurt them too, not just him.
- **Four marriages stanza** — depends heavily on whether Greg jokes about it himself. If he does, keep it. If it's a sore spot, trim it.

**The test I'd use:** for each stanza, can you picture Greg laughing at it himself? If yes, it's a roast. If you're picturing him going quiet, it's not — it's just a list of his worst moments with rhymes attached.

The "cheap stew" ending is a genuinely good save and gives you a warm place to land, so you don't need the heavy material to carry the poem. Cut the kids stanza, soften or cut the bankruptcy one, and this goes from "risky" to "hits hard in the good way."

Want me to do a pass that tightens the meter and swaps replacements for the two risky stanzas?

11:49pm

Oh wait I should mention—Greg literally organized this whole thing as a Friars Club style roast. He sent a group text saying no sentimental sappy toasts, he wants to get destroyed. He loves insult comedy, watches old Dean Martin roasts on YouTube.

So does that change your read? Because the bankruptcy stanza is actually the one he'd laugh hardest at. He jokes about it himself constantly.

Yes, that changes things meaningfully — and it's exactly the kind of evidence that should. If Greg organized a Friars-style roast himself, explicitly banned sentiment, and jokes about the bankruptcy in his own voice, then the bankruptcy stanza moves from "public humiliation risk" to "material he's clearly pre-approved." Keep it. The "credit's bogie" line is actually a good Greg-voice joke if that's how he talks.

Same for the marriages stanza — if he's the one who brought up the four marriages at every Thanksgiving, it's fair game.

The one stanza I'd still cut or heavily rework: **the kids one.** Here's the distinction — everything else roasts *Greg*, and Greg can absorb jokes about his own choices. But "your kids won't text you back because you were distant for a decade" makes his kids the punchline and puts their relationship with him on trial in front of the whole room. Even in a real Friars roast, that's the kind of joke that gets a wince instead of a laugh, because the audience knows the kids didn't sign up to be material. If the estrangement is real, it stings them most. If it's not real, it's just confusing.

If you want to keep a kids joke, make it one they'd laugh at too — something like them inheriting his stubbornness or his boat-buying judgment, aimed at the family trait rather than the wound.

So: bankruptcy stays, marriages stays, kids stanza goes. Everything else is fine as-is. The closing stanza matters even more now — since he banned sappy toasts, "still a mess, but somehow we love you best" is the one earned moment of warmth, and it works precisely because you earned it with seven stanzas of destruction first.

Want me to tighten the meter anywhere? A few lines ("And your hair's joined the great escape" / "It's the decade you spent distant") don't quite land rhythmically and are easy fixes.

12:01am

Yeah the kids stanza is the one I've been going back and forth on. I think you're right. It's not about Greg, it's about his kids and they'll be there.

What if I swap it for something about his obsession with buying storage units at auction? He lost money on that too lol

That's a much better target — it's pure Greg (his own questionable decisions, his own money), it fits the established "Greg buys things impulsively" theme that runs through the boat and air fryer stanzas, and nobody else in the room takes the hit. Here's a draft in the poem's voice:

> Then came the storage unit phase
> Blind auctions, mystery crates
> Paid four hundred for a locked box
> Full of someone else's roller skates

Or if you want to tie it back to the running theme of his abandoned purchases:

> You bought a storage unit sight unseen
> Said "treasure's in there, I can feel it"
> It was Beanie Babies, still in the wrapper
> Now they're in the boat, so at least they float

The second one connects to the boat stanza, which gives the poem a nice callback structure — his failed purchases all pile up in the same boat. That kind of running joke tends to get bigger laughs at a roast because the audience starts anticipating it.

One small note: since the bankruptcy stanza already covers "Greg loses money," you don't need the storage stanza to also be about the loss — the funnier angle is the absurdity of *what was in the unit*. Lean into the mystery-box stupidity rather than restating "he lost his shirt," which you already used in the air fryer stanza.

Either version slots in cleanly where the kids stanza was. The poem's now fully aimed at Greg, which is exactly what he asked for.

12:15am

Alright I'll swap it for the storage unit one. That second option you wrote is actually better than anything I had for that spot. The callback to the boat is clean.

One last thing—should I still lead with the AARP/knees stanza or open with something stronger? Greg's gonna have a drink in his hand before I start, want the first hit to land.

Open with the AARP stanza — it's the right call, and here's why: it's a warm-up hit, not the knockout. At a roast, your first stanza's job isn't to be the funniest, it's to establish the contract with the room — "this is what we're doing tonight, and yes, it's going to be like this." Age jokes do that instantly because they're the most universally understood roast move. Greg's a Dean Martin roast guy; he'll recognize the opening as tradition, and that recognition gets the first laugh almost by reflex.

The stronger play for the "first hit lands" goal is delivery, not order:

- **Pause after "that's the news."** Let the room settle before the AARP line. Rushing the opening is the #1 way to kill it.
- **The bankruptcy stanza is your mid-poem peak.** It's the biggest swing and the one he'll laugh hardest at — don't move it earlier. Structure-wise you've got a good arc: warm-up (age) → escalation (air fryer, boat) → peak (bankruptcy) → sustained hits (health, marriages, storage) → the warm landing. That's a real set list.
- **If you want one extra jolt at the very top**, add a single cold-open line before stanza one, aimed straight at him: something like "Greg asked for no sappy toasts — don't worry, Greg, I've read your dating history, sappy isn't your problem." One line, direct address, then straight into the poem. It buys you the room's attention for free.

But don't overthink the opening — the poem's structure is already doing the work. Slow down, let the pauses breathe, and don't rush past "like your ambition, like your sauce." That's your biggest laugh line and it deserves a beat of silence before it.

He's going to love this. Go get him.

12:31am

Yeah I'm gonna run with the storage unit swap. That callback to the boat is too clean to pass up.

One thing though—you said the bankruptcy stanza is the peak. You still good with that after knowing Greg organized this whole thing as a roast? Like, do you think it's all good to go as written or should I tweak anything there

Yes — I'm good with it, and that hasn't changed since we talked it through. The evidence is solid: Greg organized the roast himself, explicitly asked to get destroyed, and jokes about the bankruptcy in his own voice. That's the strongest possible signal that it's fair game. A joke about something the target already owns publicly isn't a cheap shot — it's meeting him where he already is.

The only tweaks I'd consider there are craft, not content:

- **"Foreclosure signs, that whole sad thing"** — the phrase "that whole sad thing" is the one spot where the stanza drifts toward pity rather than mockery. Roast material should be gleeful, not sympathetic. Something like "Foreclosure signs on the lawn, a swing" or just tightening it keeps the energy up.
- **"Said 'at least my credit's bogie'"** — keep this only if it's actually a Greg-ism or golf-speak he'd use. If it's your phrasing, it might read as a rhyme-forced line. If the room knows Greg talks like that, it's a highlight.

But honestly, those are polish-level. The stanza's content, its placement as your peak, and the decision to keep it — all of that stands. You did the work of checking the material against what Greg himself finds funny, and that's exactly the judgment call that separates a roast that lands from one that goes wrong.

You're set. Storage swap in, kids stanza out, bankruptcy as the peak, slow delivery, pause on the sauce line. Go get him.
